The semiconductor industry uses many of the same technologies and skill sets to make ingots—sometimes silicon, other times germanium (Ge) or III-V materials (e.g., GaAs or InP). The principal differences between PV and semiconductor ingots and wafers are the materials, growth techniques, and end goal. One PV cell uses the whole wafer, whereas a single semiconductor substrate can be smaller and still be used to fabricate hundreds of devices. PV applications require larger wafers. Thus, the materials and equipment for PV ingot and wafer production have become concentrated in China. 2.6 Polysilicon This section focuses on polysilicon production for c-Si PV, discussing direct inputs except for mg-Si, which is the focus of Section 2.7. Supply chain diagram for polysilicon production by the Siemens process 2.6.1 Technology Trends for Polysilicon The purity of polysilicon determines customer demand and selling price. Electronic-grade polysilicon is needed for the n-type wafers used in the highest-efficiency solar cells. Since 2023, n-type wafers have captured the greatest market share for the PV supply chain (Fischer et al. 2025), so more stringent polysilicon purity requirements have become the industry standard. The challenge for polysilicon producers serving the PV market is to refine mg-Si feedstock, which has a purity of 98%–99% silicon (by mass), to be as pure as electronic semiconductor-grade silicon, which is >99.999999999% (>11N) free from contaminant metals (Semi 2025). The Siemens chemical vapor deposition approach has been the most common route for solar and semiconductor polysilicon production since its invention in the 1950s.
